name: Dry brushing

lead: Dry brushing means stroking a firm brush over dry skin, typically before a shower. Mechanically it removes dead skin cells, which proponents say leaves skin smoother and brighter, and many also say it temporarily improves how cellulite looks.

The practice is linked to the Ayurvedic tradition of garshana and to Japanese dry towel friction, and was later adopted by Western wellness culture. Claims about smoothing and short-term circulation are tied to the mechanical action; direct studies are scarce, and claims about detoxification or lymph drainage have little scientific support according to summaries of the topic.

paras: Practitioners use a natural-fiber brush on dry skin, starting at the feet and stroking upward toward the heart, with lighter pressure on thin or sensitive areas. Sessions last about 3 to 10 minutes, often followed by a shower and moisturizer, and frequency ranges from daily to a few times a week.

It is generally considered safe when gentle. Hard brushing can cause irritation, abrasions or infection, and it is advised against on broken, inflamed or sunburned skin and with conditions like eczema or psoriasis. People with lymphatic disorders or sensitive skin are advised to consult a clinician, and brushes should be kept clean.

Temporary softening of cellulite appearance claimed
angle.text: The mechanical exfoliation is the main route to a smoother look, and some users report brighter skin and a short-term smoothing of cellulite. Effects on lymph flow and detoxification are claimed by proponents.

lead: Dry brushing is a self-care routine in which a stiff, usually natural-bristle brush is passed over dry skin, normally before bathing. It is also known as dry skin brushing and, in Ayurveda, as garshana [1].

People use it to exfoliate and smooth the skin, improve its texture and glow, and temporarily reduce the look of cellulite; proponents also credit it with boosting circulation and lymphatic drainage [1]. A related Japanese practice, kanpu masatsu, uses a dry towel for friction [1].

Direct research is limited. Summaries describe exfoliation and short-term smoothing and circulation effects as the best supported, via mechanical action, while detoxification and lasting cellulite reduction have little scientific support [1]. A German-language piece described it as an alternative skin care practice for feeling fit and revitalized [2].

paras: The routine is done on completely dry skin. Strokes move toward the heart and major lymph nodes, beginning at the feet, with gentler pressure over thin or sensitive skin [1].

Dry brushing is traced to Ayurvedic friction-based self-care and has been adapted by Western wellness culture as a standalone skincare and detox ritual [1]. Alongside it sits Japanese dry towel friction [1].

Proponents say it exfoliates, improves texture, boosts circulation, aids lymphatic drainage and detoxification, and temporarily reduces the look of cellulite [1]. Summaries of the research report that exfoliation and short-term smoothing are the best supported, that lymphatic, detox and lasting cellulite claims lack scientific support, and that direct studies are scarce [1].

Gentle brushing is generally considered safe. Excess pressure can cause irritation, abrasions or infection, and it is advised against on broken, inflamed or sunburned skin and conditions such as eczema or psoriasis; brushes need regular cleaning [1].
No studies found. Published trials of dry brushing concern a different practice, tooth cleaning, and are not about skin.
